chunks: Multiphase and heat density. The question: How do they impact heat density?
Heat density is how much power is wasted in each small area. It decides how hot a part gets.
A multiphase buck splits the loss among several stages, so each package and inductor makes much less heat, and at full load the total heat goes down too.
The heat is also spread over more board area, so the hottest spot is cooler.
Picture one big campfire versus four small fires. The campfire is intense in one spot and you must stand far away.
The small fires are each gentle, so you can put them close to things. In a multiphase buck each stage is a small fire.
The analogy has a limit: the stages sit near each other, so they warm each other a little, and the inner ones run somewhat hotter than the outer ones.
The 60 amps load on one stage or on four, built from the same parts. The single stage dissipates 8.
75 watts because its conduction loss is N squared equals 16 times one phase's; the four stages dissipate 1. 27 watts each.
The shaded halo on the left shows heat spreading from one concentrated source; the four sources on the right each have their own path to the board and a larger combined footprint.
Package size is the same in both panels.
Heat density: power dissipated per unit area. Thermal resistance ( theta ): how many degrees a part heats per watt dissipated.
Temperature rise: power times thermal resistance, change in T equals P theta . Phase: one complete buck stage ("What a multiphase buck is").
Conduction loss: I to the 2R heat, which grows with the square of the current ("Multiphase impact on efficiency").
Take the page's 60 amps load and build it from the same parts two ways. Split into four phases of 15 amps, each stage wastes about 1. 27 watts, so 5. 08 watts in total.
Put all 60 amps through one stage of those parts and it wastes about 8. 75 watts, in one package: the resistance heat grows with the square of the current.
Say each package heats 25 degrees Celsius per watt. One stage would rise 8. 75 times 25 about 219 degrees Celsius, far too hot. Each of the four rises only 1.
27 times 25 about 32 degrees Celsius. That is the whole idea: about seven times less heat per part, and less in total too.
"Heat density is watts per area, and it is what limits a part.
A single-phase 60 amp converter puts all its loss into one pair of FETs and one inductor: on the same parts that's almost 9 watts in one package.
With four phases the total is about 5 watts and each stage dissipates about 1.
3, so temperature rise, which is power times thermal resistance, drops roughly sevenfold per package, and the heat is spread over more board.

It's not a clean one over N: conduction falls faster than that per device, while neighboring phases heat each other and fixed losses grow, but the hot-spot temperature comes down, which also lowers resistance and improves efficiency."
